48.why: The text layer dropped the superscripts: the options compare with 2^20 and 2^10, not 220 and 210. Options and solution corrected; the key's B, D stands.

options.label: A
options.text: If the inputs are x=20, y=10, then the return value is greater than \(2^{20}\)

options.label: B
options.text: If the inputs are x=20, y=20, then the return value is greater than \(2^{20}\)

options.label: C
options.text: If the inputs are x=20, y=10, then the return value is less than \(2^{10}\)

options.label: D
options.text: If the inputs are x=10, y=20, then the return value is greater than \(2^{20}\)

48.solution:
Each pass of the loop does \(x \leftarrow 2x + y\), and it runs \(y\) times. Adding \(y\) to both sides, \(x + y\) doubles on every pass, so the function returns \(f(x, y) = (x + y)\cdot 2^{y} - y\).

(A) False: \(f(20, 10) = 30 \times 2^{10} - 10 = 30710\), which is less than \(2^{20} = 1048576\).

(B) True: \(f(20, 20) = 40 \times 2^{20} - 20 = 41943020 > 2^{20}\). It still fits in a 32-bit int.

(C) False: \(f(20, 10) = 30710\) is not less than \(2^{10} = 1024\).

(D) True: \(f(10, 20) = 30 \times 2^{20} - 20 = 31457260 > 2^{20}\).

So B and D.

10.why: Two independent counts of the printed figure give 5 (C); IISc's final key marks 6 (A). Key kept, notice + grace (owner policy 2026-10-29).
10.defect: IISc's final key marks 6 (option A), but the figure as printed needs 5 squares (option C), counted below.
10.solution:
Mirror every square in the line AB and count the squares that are missing.

Left shape: one square above AB in its right column; below AB, two squares side by side and one more under the right one. Its mirror image needs, above AB, a second square beside the one already there and a square above that one. That is 2 squares.

Right shape: below AB, two squares side by side and one more under the right one; nothing above. Its mirror image needs two squares side by side above AB and one more above the right one. That is 3 squares.

In all, 2 + 3 = 5 squares.

19.why:
Solution prose held '
' (the newline character), which the newline normaliser would turn into a line break; named in words instead.
19.solution: Each call reads one character into its own local a. The calls read '1', '2', '3', '4', then the fifth call reads the newline character and does not recurse; it also prints nothing. Returning, each earlier call prints its own character after the deeper call has finished: '4', then '3', '2', '1'. Output: 4321, and the program terminates.
